column2: A class of words identified through meaning, grammatical form and syntactic function. Examples: Noun: student; verb: study; article: the. Traditional notional and structural classes are distinguished in the coursebook.

A word expressing substance in the widest sense, including people, objects, materials, qualities and processes. Examples: The student opened the book. / Patience matters. Nouns can function as subject, object, predicative or attribute; noun phrases also occur within adverbial expressions.
Properties of a word’s structure and grammatical forms. Examples: book → books; student → student’s; kind → kindness. For nouns: word formation and the categories of number and case.
The positions, combinations and functions available to a word or phrase in sentences. Examples: The students arrived. / We thanked the students. A noun may head a phrase serving as subject or object.

An individual name of a particular person, place, institution or other entity. Examples: Maya lives in London. / Monday is a working day. London, Maya, Monday; article use follows established naming conventions and context.

A noun naming members of a class rather than an individual by its name. Examples: A student opened a book. / Water is essential. Kaushanskaya distinguishes class, collective, material and abstract nouns.
A common noun naming a member of a class of people, animals or things. Examples: A teacher explained the rule to three students. A student, two tables; normally countable in these senses.

A noun referring to a group or collection. Examples: The team is ready. / The police are here. / Foliage covers the path. Family-type nouns can be countable; police-type nouns require plural agreement; foliage-type nouns are generally uncountable.
A noun naming a substance or material. Examples: Gold is valuable. / The gold in this ring is recycled. Water, gold, cotton. Count uses can denote a serving, variety or object.

A noun naming a quality, state, action, idea or other abstraction. Examples: Honesty matters. / She suggested an idea. Honesty is usually uncountable; an idea is countable. Abstract meaning does not automatically imply uncountability.
A noun used in a sense which permits counting individual units. Examples: one chair → three chairs; an idea → several ideas. One idea, three ideas; a singular count noun normally needs a determiner.

A noun used in a sense without ordinary singular/plural unit counting. Examples: We need advice. / She gave me a piece of advice. Advice, furniture; use a piece of advice or an item of furniture for units.
The grammatical distinction between singular and plural forms or uses. Examples: one book → two books; one sheep → two sheep. Book/books; sheep/sheep. Meaning and agreement must also be considered.
Nouns restricted to singular grammatical use in the relevant sense. Examples: The news is encouraging. / This advice is useful. News takes singular agreement; advice has no ordinary count plural.

Nouns restricted to plural grammatical use in the relevant sense. Examples: The scissors are sharp. / A pair of trousers is missing. Scissors, trousers; a pair of scissors is singular because pair is its head.

A grammatical category expressing certain relations of a noun to other sentence elements. Examples: The student arrived. / The student’s notes are here. The traditional noun distinction is common versus genitive.
The noun form without a genitive marker. Examples: The student thanked the tutor. / The tutor thanked the student. Student, students. The form alone does not identify subject or object function.

A marked form commonly expressing possession, relationship, origin or association. Examples: Maya’s laptop; the students’ essays; children’s books. The student’s work; the students’ work; children’s books.

A genitive marker attached at the end of a phrase functioning as the possessor. Examples: The person next door’s bicycle needs repair. The person next door’s bicycle. Prefer a clearer alternative if the phrase becomes cumbersome.

A genitive used without an expressed following head noun. Examples: This laptop is Maya’s. / We met at the dentist’s. This is Maya’s; at the dentist’s. Also called absolute genitive in traditional descriptions.

A construction combining of with a genitive form or independent possessive. Examples: A friend of Maya’s called. / A colleague of mine is presenting. A friend of Maya’s; a colleague of mine. Its meaning and restrictions differ from ordinary of-phrases.

A system of grammatical classification related to distinctions such as masculine, feminine and neuter. Examples: The teacher said they would return. / The woman introduced herself. English nouns generally lack productive grammatical gender inflection; reference and pronoun choice remain relevant.
A noun with a single root and no derivational affix in the analysis used here. Examples: book; table; phone. Book, table.
A noun formed through derivational affixation. Examples: kind → kindness; teach → teacher; happy → unhappiness. Kindness, teacher, unhappiness.
A noun formed from two or more bases. Examples: bookshelf; mother-in-law; swimming pool. Bookshelf, mother-in-law; spelling may be solid, hyphenated or open.
The sentence element typically identifying what the predication is about and controlling agreement. Examples: The students have arrived. The students have arrived.
A complement selected by a verb or, in traditional analysis, a preposition. Examples: They discussed the report. / They relied on the guide. They discussed the report; they spoke about the report.
A complement attributing an identity, role or property to the subject after a linking verb. Examples: Maya is a researcher. Maya is a researcher.
An element modifying a noun. Examples: A grammar lesson; the cover of the book. A grammar lesson; the cover of the book.

In traditional analysis, an object introduced by a preposition and linked to the governing word. Examples: They relied on the guide. / She listened to the speaker. They relied on the guide. Distinguish it from an optional place or time modifier.

An element expressing a circumstance such as place, time, manner, reason or purpose. Examples: They met after lunch. / She worked in the library. They met after lunch. Analyse the entire phrase before identifying the noun inside it.

A structural word used with nouns in the traditional classification. Examples: A student entered. The student sat down. Students need feedback. A/an is indefinite; the is definite. Zero article describes the absence of an overt article in relevant constructions.

A/an introduces a singular count referent as a member of a class or in a non-identifying use. Examples: A university offers courses. / An hour has sixty minutes. A university; an hour. Choose the form by sound.

The signals that the intended referent can be identified in the context, or occurs in established generic and naming patterns. Examples: Please send the report you mentioned. The report you requested; the sun.

The absence of an overt article in a construction where article choice is relevant. Examples: Water is essential. / Students need feedback. / Go to school. Water is essential; students need feedback; go to school.
Presenting a referent as a member of a class. Examples: She is a linguist. / This is a useful tool. She is a linguist.
Identifying a referent as the particular one intended in the context. Examples: The linguist who led our seminar works here. The linguist who led our seminar.

Reference to a class, kind or general phenomenon rather than one particular instance. Examples: Books are useful. / The tiger is endangered. Books are useful; the tiger is endangered. Different generic constructions are not always interchangeable.
A modifier adding a description without necessarily making the referent uniquely identifiable. Examples: We need a helpful colleague. / Cold water is refreshing. A helpful colleague; cold water.

A modifier which, in context, helps identify the particular referent intended. Examples: The colleague who chairs our department has arrived. The colleague who chairs our department; the water in this bottle. A modifier does not mechanically require the.
A part of speech which points out objects and their qualities without naming them. Examples: Maya arrived. She waved. / This is useful. Kaushanskaya, Chapter IV §1.

Pronouns referring to the speaker, addressee, or people and things spoken about. Examples: I thanked her. / They spoke to us. I/me, you, he/him, she/her, it, we/us, they/them; distinguish person, number and case.

Forms expressing possession or association, with conjoint and absolute forms. Examples: These are my notes. Those are yours. my/mine, your/yours, her/hers, our/ours, their/theirs; his has the same form. Modern accounts often call my a determiner.

Forms referring back to the subject when the action returns to or is associated with the doer. Examples: Maya introduced herself. / We checked ourselves. She introduced herself. The same forms have emphatic uses: She herself introduced the speaker.

Each other and one another express mutual action or relationship. Examples: They helped each other. / We read one another’s comments. They checked each other’s answers. Modern usage does not enforce a two-versus-more-than-two distinction.
Forms pointing out people, things or ideas. Examples: This is my draft. Those are yours. / We chose the same. This, that, these, those; Kaushanskaya also includes such and (the) same.
Pronouns pointing out a person or thing indefinitely. Examples: Someone called. / Is there anything to add? Some, any and their compounds; one. Interpretation depends on context.
Forms expressing absence or exclusion of people or things. Examples: Nobody replied. / Neither option works. / We have none. No, none, nobody, no one, nothing, neither.

In classifications using this label, forms identifying something different, separate or additional. Examples: We need another example. / One is ready; the other needs work. Typically other and another. This is an additional teaching label: Kaushanskaya groups them under defining pronouns.

In classifications using this label, forms referring to a whole set or distributing reference over its members. Examples: All are welcome. / Each student has a copy. / Both agreed. All, both, each, every and every-compounds; membership varies by classification. Kaushanskaya includes these under defining pronouns.
Pronouns used in inquiry to form special questions. Examples: Who called? / Which topic do you prefer? Who, whose, what, which; whom is an objective form of who.

Pronouns introducing subject, object or predicative subordinate clauses and functioning within those clauses. Examples: I know who called. / What you need is a clear example. Kaushanskaya’s analysis: I know who called. Who is subject of called; the clause is object of know.

Pronouns connecting a relative clause to its antecedent and functioning within that clause; some refer to a preceding clause. Examples: The student who called is here. / The draft that we read was useful. The student who called. Who is subject within the relative clause.
A part of speech indicating number or the order of people and things in a series. Examples: Three students arrived. / She finished third. Kaushanskaya, Chapter V §1.
Numerals indicating exact number and used in counting. Examples: one; twelve; twenty-three; a hundred. One, twelve, forty, a hundred, twenty-three.
Numerals indicating position or order in a series. Examples: first; fifth; ninth; twelfth; twenty-first. First, second, third, fifth, ninth, twelfth, twenty-first.
Numbers expressible as a numerator divided by a non-zero denominator. Examples: 3/4 = three quarters; 2/3 = two thirds. Three quarters: 3/4. Mathematical definition supplied for this course.
A fraction with a power of ten as denominator, expressible in decimal notation. Examples: 0.375 = zero point three seven five. 375/1000 = 0.375: zero point three seven five.
The upper number in a common fraction. Examples: In 3/4, the numerator is 3. In 3/4, the numerator is 3. In a part–whole model it counts the parts taken.
The lower, non-zero number in a common fraction. Examples: In 3/4, the denominator is 4. In 3/4, the denominator is 4. In a part–whole model it indicates the equal parts making a whole.

The person, thing, situation or idea that an expression refers to in a particular context. Examples: In Maya arrived. She waved, the referent of she is the person Maya. In Maya arrived. She waved, both Maya and she refer to the same person: that person is their referent.

A linguistic expression which provides the interpretation of another expression, commonly a pronoun. Examples: In Maya arrived. She waved, the expression Maya is the antecedent of she. In Maya arrived. She waved, the written expression Maya is the antecedent of she. The person Maya is the referent.

A subordinate clause that modifies a nominal expression or adds a comment about a preceding clause. Examples: The student who called is here. / The session ended early, which surprised us. The student who called is here. / The session ended early, which surprised us.

A relative clause that helps identify or restrict the referent of its antecedent, integrated into the noun phrase. Examples: The students who submitted early received feedback. The students who submitted early received feedback. No separating commas; this identifies a subset.

A supplementary relative clause adding information about an already identified referent. Examples: Maya, who submitted early, received feedback. Maya, who submitted early, received feedback. Set it off with commas; do not use that or omit the relative pronoun.

column1: Emphatic use of a reflexive form
column2: Use of a reflexive form to emphasise the identity or personal involvement of a participant rather than fill an ordinary reflexive object position. Examples: Maya herself approved the plan. / We prepared the slides ourselves. Maya herself approved the plan. Compare Maya introduced herself, where herself is a reflexive object.

It used to occupy a grammatical position without referring to an ordinary person or thing. Examples: It is raining. / It is important to check the figures. It is raining. / It is important to check the figures. Compare The projector is ready. It works, where it has a referent.
